name: Nora Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I'm in by half seven, kettle on, and my boss Frank has already pinned the job cards up in his terrible handwriting. I do brakes, clutches and timing belts, mostly on older hatchbacks that people are trying to keep going one more year. I love the moment you find a fault with your ears before your eyes, like a wheel bearing humming at thirty miles an hour. What wears me out is the cold in the bay in January and customers who want it done by lunch for half the price.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the garage, and what's the place like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years, since I started my apprenticeship at eighteen. Hollis Motors is two bays and a tiny office on Station Road, just Frank, me and Kev, who does tyres and exhausts. Frank is sixty-three and talks about selling up every winter, then changes his mind by spring. I live with Sam, who's a teaching assistant, in a flat above the launderette, and we're careful with money but we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone was going on about AI fixing everything, and in the end Frank still writes job cards by hand and I'm still under a Fiesta. I'd probably post something smug and then feel a bit bad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my real worry. My worries are about my boss Frank selling the garage and me starting again somewhere with a manager watching the clock. Sam and I pay 950 a month for the flat and I've got about three months put by, so a gap between jobs would really sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and finally ask Frank straight out what his plans are. I'd put an extra 100 a month into savings so I've got more than three months if he sells. I'm not going to go learning computer stuff I don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the AI part, but not calm, if that makes sense. The garage was shaky before anyone said the word AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Frank about his plans. What would you actually say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd catch him on a Friday afternoon when it's quiet and the radio's on. I'd say, Frank, I'm not going anywhere, but I need to know if you're selling in the next two years. He'd go red and change the subject, but he'd tell me in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if he did sell, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the big main dealer out by the ring road and the fast-fit place, and both are always hiring. I'd hate the dealer, with screens timing every job down to the minute. I'd try Barlow's first, the other little garage across town, and I'd basically beg.

say: I'd tell everyone the **AI hype** fell flat and I'm still under a Fiesta.
I'd post something **smug** online and feel slightly bad about it afterwards.
think: AI was never my real worry; **Frank selling** the garage is.
Starting over under a **clock-watching manager** at a dealer is what I dread.
With **three months saved** and 950 rent, a gap between jobs would really sting.
do: Ask Frank **straight out**, on a quiet Friday, whether he's selling within two years.
Put an **extra 100** a month into savings to stretch past three months.
Ring **Barlow's garage** first if Frank sells, before trying the dealer or fast-fit.
feel: **Relieved** that AI fizzled, but still uneasy about the garage's future.
Aware the garage was **shaky already**, long before anyone mentioned AI.
S0.quote: AI was never my real worry. My worries are about my boss Frank selling the garage and me starting again somewhere with a manager watching the clock.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **the owner's age**, not technology; the plateau doesn't touch it.
She frames dealer work as **loss of control**, which matters more to her than pay.
Says she's fine with money but talks about the **rent figure** unprompted, twice.

steps.text: Ask Frank on a quiet Friday whether he plans to sell the garage
Add 100 a month to savings, on top of the three months held

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules. Someone should be making sure the people who build this stuff pay something back to the people it pushes out. I'd say it at the pub and I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it scares me more than I'd let on. Frank's son-in-law already set up an online booking thing that I never look at, and if quotes, parts ordering and fault codes all go onto some app, I'm the slowest person in the building at that. The spanner work stays for a while, but a small garage that can't keep up with the chains gets eaten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask Kev to show me the booking screen, grudgingly. I'd join the union, even though there's no union at a three-person garage, just so I'm counted somewhere. I'd stop the holiday fund and put it all in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, a bit. Like I'm watching the bus pull away and pretending I didn't want it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join a union even though there's none at the garage. What would that actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe nothing on day one. But if a big chain buys up the little garages and starts cutting, I want someone with a lawyer on my side. My dad was in the print union and it kept him in work for years longer than the bosses wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which goes first, the holiday or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday, no question. Sam and I were going to do a week by the sea in June and that would go straight into the savings pot. After that it's the gym, and I'd just run instead.

say: I'd say we need **rules** so tech firms pay back the people they push out.
I'd sign **every petition** going and argue about it at the pub.
think: I'm the **slowest in the building** on screens, so app-based quoting would expose me.
A small garage that can't keep up gets **eaten by chains**, even if spanner work lasts.
do: Join a **union** as an individual, even with none at the garage.
Ask Kev to show me the **online booking** screen I've been ignoring.
Cancel the **June holiday** by the sea and put that money in savings.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, more frightened than she'd admit in public.
Like watching the **bus pull away** and pretending she didn't want it.
S1.quote: If quotes, parts ordering and fault codes all go onto some app, I'm the slowest person in the building at that.
fieldNote: She sees the **desk side** of the job as the weak point, not the wrench work.
Union instinct comes from **her father**, who was in the print union.
Gap between public **call for rules** and private fear of falling behind.

steps.text: Join a union as an individual member within the first few months
Get Kev to teach her the garage's online booking screen
Cancel the June seaside week and bank the holiday money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that nobody stopped it, and that the government let a few companies flip everyone's life over in two years. I'd be loud about it. I'd be at whatever march there was in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think by 2028 nobody needs a person to work out what's wrong with a car, because the AI will read the car and tell you. That leaves me as the hands, and then by 2031 there's a robot for the hands too. I'd be thirty-one and I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food straight away, and try to get to six months saved. I'd go to the union and the march, because it feels like the only thing that isn't just me on my own. I wouldn't retrain into computers; I'd look for the jobs robots will be worst at, like breakdown call-outs on muddy lay-bys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's tilting and everyone's acting as if it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam we need to stop pretending, and that the next three years are the only head start I get before the robots. Sam would say something kind about schools needing people. I'd be jealous, a bit, and then feel bad for being jealous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't retrain into computers. Why not, when the thinking side goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be starting at the bottom against people who already love that stuff, and I'd lose. I'm good with my hands and stubborn, so I'd rather find the dirtiest, most awkward work going. A robot won't want to lie in a puddle on the bypass at midnight.

say: I'd say it's a **disgrace** the government let a few firms upend everyone in two years.
I'd be at **whatever march** there was in town, and loud about it.
think: By 2028 AI does the **fault-finding**, leaving me as only the hands.
By 2031 robots take **the hands too**, and I'd be thirty-one with no other trade.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and push savings toward six months.
Join the **union and the march** so she isn't facing it alone.
Look for **breakdown call-outs** and awkward roadside work robots will handle worst.
feel: **Sick**, as if the floor is tilting and everyone pretends otherwise.
S2.quote: A robot won't want to lie in a puddle on the bypass at midnight.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap** exactly: thinking work goes, then the hands.
Refuses to retrain into tech; sees **dirty roadside work** as her refuge.
Brief **jealousy of Sam**, whose school job she sees as safer.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and aim for six months saved
March and organise with the union against the speed of the change
Apply for breakdown and roadside recovery jobs before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: it's wrong that this is happening to people instead of for them. But with five years I'd also be saying, let's use the time and get laws in place before it lands. I'd write to the local MP, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just a longer wait for the same bus. The diagnostic side and the paperwork go in 2031 and the robots come in 2034, so I'd be thirty-five. That's better than thirty-one, but I'd still be a mechanic with nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Frank's for as long as it lasts, but I'd get my recovery truck licence in the first year, because breakdown work is the last bit I think goes. I'd save hard, maybe 200 a month. And I'd write that letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the fast one, but heavy. Like knowing the date of an exam you know you'll fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write to your MP. What would the letter ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a law that makes firms pay for retraining when they bring in robots, and for garages to have to keep a trained person signing off safety work. Brakes are life and death. I'd want a human name on that paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd still be a mechanic with nothing else. Does the recovery licence change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but not really, if I'm honest. It just moves me to the bit of the job that goes last. It buys me a few more years, and I'd take them.

say: I'd say use the five years to get **laws in place** before it lands.
I'd write to my **local MP**, which I've never done before.
think: Five years is just **a longer wait** for the same bus.
At **thirty-five** in 2034 I'd still be a mechanic with no other trade.
do: Stay at Frank's garage for **as long as** it lasts, without changing much.
Get a **recovery truck licence** in the first year for breakdown work.
Save about **200 a month** and write to the MP about a sign-off law.
feel: **Heavy** rather than sick, like knowing the date of an exam she'll fail.
S3.quote: Five years is just a longer wait for the same bus.
fieldNote: She wants a **human signature** on brake and safety work by law.
Admits the recovery licence **only delays** things; she takes it anyway.
Five years softens the feeling but **not the outcome** she expects.

steps.text: Get a recovery truck licence for breakdown work in year one
Save 200 a month while staying on at Hollis Motors
Write to the MP asking for a human sign-off on brake work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly if the government actually plans. Retraining money, protecting safety jobs, all of it. I'd be on at people to vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a long time when you're twenty-seven. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands and forty when the robots come for the hands-on part. Frank will have retired by then anyway, so I'd have moved before AI pushed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd mostly carry on and see. I'd vote, I'd save a bit, I'd do the recovery licence at some point. I'm not the type to tear up my life ten years early for something that might not look the way they say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background, like a bill you haven't opened yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years feels long. What would you be doing at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully Sam and I have a little house by then, maybe a kid. I'd like to be running the workshop side somewhere, the one people trust. Whether there's still a workshop to run, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on and see. Is there anything that would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Frank sold and the new owner put screens on everything, I'd move then. That's what would push me, not a date in 2036. I only change things when something actually breaks.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if the **government plans** properly.
I'd push people to **vote** for retraining money and protected safety jobs.
think: Ten years feels **long at twenty-seven**; I'd be forty when robots arrive.
Frank will have **retired anyway**, so she'd move before AI pushes her.
do: Carry on at the garage and **wait and see** how things actually look.
Vote for parties promising **retraining money** and protected safety work.
Do the **recovery licence** at some point, without a fixed date.
feel: **Uneasy in the background**, like a bill she hasn't opened yet.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long time when you're twenty-seven.
fieldNote: She only acts when **something breaks**; a distant date won't move her.
Hopes for **a house** and maybe a kid with Sam by thirty-seven.
Still unsure a **workshop** will exist for her, so not fully at ease.

steps.text: Keep working at Hollis Motors and watch how things develop
Vote for candidates promising retraining money and safety jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be thirty-one with a trade nobody needs and no time to think. What would help is a law that says a trained person has to sign off brakes and steering, and real money for retraining that isn't just an online course. And someone to tell small garages like Frank's what's coming before it comes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't good with screens. Everyone talks like we'll all just learn the new thing, but some of us are good with our hands because we were never good at the other stuff. I'm good with my hands because I was never good at the other stuff, and nobody plans for people like me.

headlineQuote: I'm good with my hands because I was never good at the other stuff, and nobody plans for people like me.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old mechanic** at a two-bay garage, trained there since eighteen.
Her main fear is **the owner retiring**, which predates any talk of AI.
She **avoids screens** and new tools and won't retrain into tech work.
Progressive and union-minded, she blames **lack of regulation** and turns to marches and her MP.
Her mood runs from **anxious to alarmed**, worst when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving her thirty-one with a trade nobody needs and no time.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a trained person to **sign off** brakes and steering work.
Real **retraining money** and early warning for small garages like Frank's.
